title: Engineer's Lexicon
sub: Terms every software engineer should own.

cards.def: Caching a function's results so repeated calls with the same input are fast.
examples: Memoization cut the recursive Fibonacci from exponential to linear time.
We added memoization to the price calculator to avoid repeat work.
Memoization trades memory for speed.
The interviewer asked me to improve the solution with memoization.

cards.def: Bundling data with the methods that operate on it and restricting outside access.
examples: Encapsulation keeps the account balance private.
Encapsulation means other classes can't change the balance directly.
Good encapsulation makes code easier to change safely.
We broke encapsulation by making every field public.

cards.def: A lock ensuring only one thread accesses a resource at a time.
examples: Guard the shared counter with a mutex.
Two threads waited forever because each held a mutex the other needed.
Release the mutex as soon as the update is done.
A mutex prevents two users from booking the same seat at once.

cards.def: Accumulated mess that makes the next change harder than it should be.
examples: Refactoring debt slowed every feature in the legacy module.
We set aside time each sprint to pay down refactoring debt.
Refactoring debt builds up when deadlines are always tight.
New joiners struggle most with code full of refactoring debt.

cards.def: A pattern considered natural and conventional in a language.
examples: Using list comprehensions is the Pythonic idiom.
Using try-with-resources is the Java idiom for closing files.
Learn the idioms of a language, not just its syntax.
Code reviewers asked me to follow the team's idiom for error handling.

cards.def: Averaged over many operations rather than the worst single case.
examples: Appending to a dynamic array is amortized O(1).
The amortized cost of each insert is low, even if some are slow.
Amortized analysis looks at the average over many operations.
Hash table lookups are amortized constant time.

cards.def: Converting an object into a format that can be stored or transmitted.
examples: Serialization to JSON broke on circular references.
Serialization lets us save the game state to a file.
Choose a serialization format that other teams can read.
Slow serialization was the hidden cost in our API.

cards.def: Software that sits between a request and the handler to add shared behavior.
examples: Auth is applied as middleware on every route.
We added logging middleware to record every request.
The middleware checks the user's language before the page loads.
Keep middleware small, because it runs on every call.

cards.def: Restricting how many requests a client may make in a time window.
examples: Rate limiting stopped the scraper.
Rate limiting protects the login page from password attacks.
The API returns a 429 error when rate limiting kicks in.
We relaxed rate limiting for our biggest customers.

cards.def: A tool that analyzes code for style problems and likely bugs.
examples: The linter caught an unused variable.
Run the linter before you open a pull request.
Our linter enforces one style across the team.
The linter warned about a possible null value.

cards.def: A chain of small tasks you must do before the one you actually wanted.
examples: Updating the toolchain turned into days of yak shaving.
I wanted to fix one bug but ended up yak shaving all afternoon.
Yak shaving is common when setting up a new laptop.
Stop yak shaving and ask someone for help.
